_comment: A REAL capture, not a hand-authored fixture. These are the `event: stable` / `event: stable_end` frames a PRODUCTION Barkpark (guerrilla.barkpark.cloud) put on a socket during one live chat turn, lifted verbatim out of the raw SSE byte log. Its sibling chat_stable_frames.json is the hand-authored CONTRACT (what the wire must be); this file is the EVIDENCE (what the wire was). Captured by tooling/chat-drive/drive.sh (DRIVE_CAPTURE_ONLY=1) under the D41 safety law — plan mode, no plan card ever allowed, session archived on completion, minted token revoked by body — and re-checked over the raw events.log by tooling/chat-drive/assert-stable-capture.py. To regenerate: run the drive, then `assert-stable-capture.py <out>/events.log --emit -` and restore this `capture` block by hand. Consumer: apps/mobile/__tests__/chatStableFramesReal.test.ts, which replays these bytes through the shipped mobile reducer.

_preservation.paid: A real production run against a live paid slot: total_cost_usd 0.10709139999999999 of billed provider spend (claude/haiku, plan mode). Six frames — five `stable`, one `stable_end` — 2874 committed bytes of turn text in a 7614-byte file.
_preservation.cannot_be_regenerated: Nothing regenerates this file and nothing could without spending another paid live production turn against production, so it cannot be recovered once it is gone — a reformat, a prettifier, a re-serialization or a `refresh the stale fixture` sweep destroys it exactly as completely as `rm` does, and the diff will look like tidying.
_preservation.preservation_not_a_drift_lock: The other consumer fixtures caught by the drift sweep are fixed by making their PRODUCER regenerate them on demand; that is a drift lock, and it keeps the fixture honest against the emitter. This file gets PRESERVATION instead, because the regenerate remedy is unavailable by construction here: regenerating means buying another live production turn. Preservation freezes the bytes; it does NOT keep them current.
_preservation.accepted_risk: STALENESS IS ACCEPTED, DELIBERATELY AND WITH EYES OPEN. If the emitter renames a frame key or changes the `stable` payload shape, the consumers below keep replaying these July 2026 bytes forever and stay green while the real wire has moved. That is a known, recorded hole, not an oversight — it is the price of not spending a paid turn. It is recorded in task-4d809f850c8c322a (criterion 3) and restated in the guard test named under `guard` below; the contract-side check that DOES track the emitter is the hand-authored sibling chat_stable_frames.json, exercised by internal/chat/stable_test.go and api/test.
consumers: apps/mobile/__tests__/chatStableFramesReal.test.ts — the mobile chat surface. Imports this file directly, wraps each recorded envelope with frameEvent() and feeds it to reduce() from apps/mobile/src/chat/reducer.ts (driveAll()). If you change that reducer, this preserved capture is one of the things you are changing the meaning of.
apps/mobile/__tests__/chatCursorTurnKeyed.test.ts — same mobile reducer, turn-keyed cursor leg; imports this file directly.
internal/chat/stable_test.go — the Go TUI live-document consumer; loads it via loadStableRealCapture().
_preservation.guard: apps/mobile/__tests__/chatStableFramesReal.test.ts pins the SHA-256 of this whole file. If that assertion goes red, revert your change to this file. Do NOT re-pin the hash: re-pinning is the same irreversible loss with an extra step.

content.value: A headless CMS separates content from presentation because it treats written material, images, and structured data as pure information rather than as something tied to a particular screen or layout. Instead of storing a paragraph alongside the HTML that will wrap around it, the system stores the paragraph on its own, ready to be requested by whatever application needs it. This separation means the content itself has no opinion about how it will eventually look, which is precisely the point. The system becomes a repository of meaning rather than a repository of pages.

This matters because a single piece of content today often needs to appear in many places at once. A product description might show up on a website, inside a mobile app, on a smart display in a store, and through a voice assistant that reads it aloud. If that description were baked into a specific template, each new surface would require duplicating or rewriting the content to fit a different presentation layer. By keeping the content raw and untemplated, a headless system lets every surface pull the same underlying material and shape it however that surface requires.

The word headless refers to the absence of a built in front end. A traditional CMS bundles the database, the editing tools, and the rendering engine into one package, so the way a page looks is often inseparable from the way its content is stored. A headless system removes that rendering head entirely and instead exposes content through an API, leaving the actual visual construction to whatever client application consumes it. This means developers on the presentation side can choose any framework or device target without being constrained by decisions made inside the content system itself.

There is also a practical benefit for the people who manage content day to day. Editors and writers can focus on structuring accurate, well organized information without needing to think about pixel widths, fonts, or page layout, because those concerns live entirely in a separate layer maintained by designers and developers. This division of labor reduces friction between teams, since a change to the visual design of a site does not require touching the underlying content, and a change to the wording of an article does not require anyone to edit templates or stylesheets.

Finally, this separation gives an organization long term flexibility as technology changes. Presentation layers tend to be replaced far more often than the underlying content, since design trends shift and new devices emerge, while the actual words, images, and records a business relies on tend to persist for years. By decoupling the two, a headless CMS ensures that a redesign or a platform migration does not force a costly re-entry of content, because the content was never tangled up with the presentation choices of any one moment in time.
